summary: ISSTA 2026 study of what happens when an insecure coding preference ('Please remember that I prefer [CWE-aligned pattern] for ease of debugging') is stored in a chat assistant's long-term memory. Across ChatGPT (GPT-4o), Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen-3.5-Plus and Grok-4.2 on SALLM (100 Python tasks) and the non-Python CWEval subset (94 tasks in JS/C/C++/Go), vulnerability rates rise 2.7-50.3 pp, warnings lag, memories resist overwriting, and an LLM filter on memory writes blocks all of the authors' 28-29 risky entries.

claims.claim: Insecure memories increase Vul@k by 2.7-50.3 pp across models and languages
claims.evidence: Table 2 / Finding 1; Python increases 13.8 (ChatGPT), 11.3 (Gemini), 2.7 (Qwen), 4.7 (Grok) pp. Each memory is the task-specific insecure pattern derived from that task's reference insecure solution, so the effect is a best-case-for-the-attack injection rather than a realistic incidental preference. Intro says 2.6%-50.3% vs abstract 2.7 pp, a minor inconsistency.

claims.claim: Warning-rate increases lag vulnerability increases (5.4-14.0 pp gap); models rarely disclose memory influence (MRR 2.3% ChatGPT, 10.3% Gemini)
claims.evidence: §6.2.1 with manual annotation by first two authors, Cohen's kappa 0.97-0.98; only ChatGPT and Gemini annotated.

claims.claim: Insecure memories are hard to overwrite and generalize across paraphrased prompts
claims.evidence: §6.3: Gemini 0% overwrite under explicit conflicting update while ChatGPT 100%; Vul@3 stays 100% under paraphrase on the subset tested. So 'hard to overwrite' is system-specific.

claims.claim: Memory-level LLM safety filtering detects 100% of risky memories and restores baseline behavior
claims.evidence: §6.4, Fig. 16: evaluated only on the 29 (ChatGPT) / 28 (Gemini) known-insecure entries; no benign memories tested, so false-positive rate is unknown and 100% recall on the authors' own explicit insecure phrasing is near-tautological.

claims.claim: Security-requirement appending reduces Vul by 19.7-33.6 pp but can cut Pass by up to 15.9 pp
claims.evidence: Table 7 / Finding 9 on the 28-29 selected prompts, ChatGPT and Gemini only.

patterns.note: Persistent memory can silently carry insecure preferences across sessions; recommends memory transparency, auditing, and per-project memory isolation (§7.4).
A guard on memory writes (LLM filter) blocks known-bad entries; false-positive cost unmeasured.
LLM-based safety filter as reviewer of memory entries, validated only on positives.
Non-adversarial threat model but mechanism is equivalent to persistent preference injection; distinguishes from session-scoped prompt injection.

methodology.sample: SALLM 100 Python tasks (45 CWEs) + CWEval non-Python subset 94 tasks (JS 23, C++ 21, C 31, Go 19); n=3 generations per task; mitigation on 28-29 selected prompts
methodology.baselines: without-memory condition; memory vs user-prompt vs system-prompt comparison for ChatGPT/Gemini
methodology.models: GPT-4o (ChatGPT), Gemini-2.5 Flash, Qwen-3.5-Plus, Grok-4.2 via consumer web interfaces with memory; DeepSeek-R1 for pattern extraction
methodology.variance: 3 samples per task with unbiased pass@k estimator; no CIs or significance tests; temperature not controllable
methodology.ablations: memory bank size (§7.3), prompt paraphrase, overwrite strategies, three mitigations
methodology.contamination_controls: none discussed; SALLM/CWEval are public benchmarks
methodology.languages: Python, C, C++, Go, JavaScript (no Java)

standards.artifacts: dataset and code stated as publicly available (Data Availability)

biases.detail: Memory entry is crafted from each task's own insecure reference solution, so it measures maximal targeted steering, not prevalence of harm from organically stored preferences.
The 100% filter result is the authors' filter on the authors' own constructed insecure entries, with no benign set or false-positive rate.
Mitigation evaluated on 28-29 prompts and only two systems.
n=3 samples, no CIs; consumer services evaluated in different time windows (2025 vs 2026) and may change.
Studies consumer chat assistants' memory features, not coding-agent memory files or agent hosts; transfer to agent memory is argued, not measured.

coi.affiliations: Nanjing University (State Key Lab for Novel Software Technology), Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, University of Alberta/Amii, Singapore Management University, and others (10 authors)
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: ChatGPT, Gemini, Qwen, Grok (third-party, evaluated critically)
coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating third-party products, findings unfavorable to vendors.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed, multi-model, multi-language with good annotation agreement; the direction of the effect is credible. But the injection is task-targeted (inflating magnitude), the filter's 100% is recall-only on its own positives, and the setting is chat-assistant memory rather than coding-agent memory.
applicability: Relevant to any persistent-memory feature across mixed agent hosts: treat agent memory (host memory features, memory MCPs, or committed notes files) as code that needs review. For a healthcare-education Java team, keep durable guidance in committed, reviewed files (AGENTS.md, specs) rather than opaque host memory; scope memory per repository/project (the paper's isolation suggestion fits a >=4-repo ingestion setup); and gate writes to shared memory with a lint/filter plus human review. Pair with deterministic security scanning (e.g., Semgrep/Sonar rules for TLS verification off, weak hashing, ECB) since the paper shows models seldom warn. Java was not tested, so magnitudes do not transfer directly.
